claim: Maternal genetic effects can be defined as the effect of a mother's genotype on the phenotype of her offspring, independent of the offspring's genotype.
source: Maternal genetic effects can be defined as the effect of a mother's genotype on the phenotype of her offspring, independent of the offspring's genotype.
evidence: This is a definitional statement that establishes the meaning of maternal genetic effects for the manuscript.

claim: Maternal genetic effects can act via the intrauterine environment during pregnancy and/or via the postnatal environment.
source: Maternal genetic effects can act via the intrauterine environment during pregnancy and/or via the postnatal environment.
evidence: This statement describes the pathways through which maternal genetic effects operate, drawing on established understanding.

claim: The manuscript presents a structural equation modelling (SEM) extension to the basic adoption design that partitions maternal genetic effects into prenatal and postnatal effects.
source: In this manuscript, we present a simple extension to the basic adoption design that uses structural equation modelling (SEM) to partition maternal genetic effects into prenatal and postnatal effects.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the methodological contribution of the manuscript.

claim: The model was applied to polygenic scores of educational attainment and birth weight associated variants in up to 5,178 adopted singletons, 943 trios, 2687 mother-offspring pairs, 712 father-offspring pairs and 347,980 singletons from the UK Biobank.
source: We apply our model to polygenic scores of educational attainment and birth weight associated variants, in up to 5,178 adopted singletons, 943 trios, 2687 mother-offspring pairs, 712 father-offspring pairs and 347,980 singletons from the UK Biobank.
evidence: This describes the empirical application of the model with specific sample sizes from UK Biobank data.

claim: The results show the expected pattern of maternal genetic effects on offspring birth weight.
source: Our results show the expected pattern of maternal genetic effects on offspring birth weight, but unexpectedly large prenatal maternal genetic effects on offspring educational attainment.
evidence: This is a summary statement of empirical findings from the analysis.

claim: The results show unexpectedly large prenatal maternal genetic effects on offspring educational attainment.
source: Our results show the expected pattern of maternal genetic effects on offspring birth weight, but unexpectedly large prenatal maternal genetic effects on offspring educational attainment.
evidence: This is a summary statement of empirical findings that contradicts expectations.

claim: Sensitivity and simulation analyses suggest the unexpected result for educational attainment may be at least partially due to adopted individuals in the UK Biobank being raised by their biological relatives.
source: Sensitivity and simulation analyses suggest this result may be at least partially due to adopted individuals in the UK Biobank being raised by their biological relatives.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on additional analyses (sensitivity and simulation) performed in the study.

claim: Accurate modelling of cryptic relationships is sufficient to bring type I error rate under control and produce asymptotically unbiased estimates of prenatal and postnatal maternal genetic effects.
source: We show that accurate modelling of these sorts of cryptic relationships is sufficient to bring type I error rate under control and produce asymptotically unbiased estimates of prenatal and postnatal maternal genetic effects.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on simulation studies described in the manuscript.

claim: Over the last few years there has been a resurgence of interest in identifying and quantifying maternal genetic effects on offspring phenotypes.
source: Over the last few years there has been a resurgence of interest in identifying and quantifying maternal genetic effects on offspring phenotypes, both from the perspective of variance component estimation (Balbona et al., 2021; Bates et al., 2018; Eaves et al., 2014; Eilertsen et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2021; Kong et al., 2018; Qiao et al., 2020; Tubbs et al., 2020) and estimating the causal effect of specific maternal environmental exposures on offspring outcomes through Mendelian randomization based approaches (Evans et al., 2019; Lawlor et al., 2017; Moen et al., 2020; Tyrrell et al., 2016; Warrington et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to recent literature.

claim: Following the advent of transgenerational genome-wide association studies, maternal genetic effects are beginning to be identified at individual genetic loci.
source: Indeed, following the advent of transgenerational genome-wide association studies, maternal genetic effects are beginning to be identified at individual genetic loci (Warrington et al., 2019; Beaumont et al., 2018), a trend that is set to continue as the sample sizes of such studies increase further.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to specific GWAS studies.

claim: Resolving maternal effects into prenatal and postnatal sources of variation could be a valuable first step in eventually elucidating the underlying mechanisms behind these associations.
source: Indeed, resolving maternal effects into prenatal and postnatal sources of variation could be a valuable first step in eventually elucidating the underlying mechanisms behind these associations (Armstrong-Carter et al., 2020), directing investigators to where they should focus their attention, and in the case of disease-related phenotypes, yielding potentially important information regarding the optimal timing of interventions.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential value of the approach, supported by a citation.

claim: An adopted individual's phenotype is influenced by prenatal intrauterine factors as proxied by their biological mother's genome, and postnatal influences as proxied by their adoptive mother's and father's genomes.
source: We assume that an adopted individual's phenotype is influenced by prenatal intrauterine factors as proxied by their biological mother's genome, and postnatal influences as proxied by their adoptive mother's and father's genomes.
evidence: This is a fundamental assumption of the model described in the manuscript.

claim: The phenotype of individuals who have not been adopted are influenced by prenatal intrauterine factors resulting from their biological mother's genome, and postnatal factors as proxied by their biological mother's and father's genomes.
source: In contrast, we assume that the phenotype of individuals who have not been adopted are influenced by prenatal intrauterine factors resulting from their biological mother's genome, and postnatal factors as proxied by their biological mother's and father's genomes.
evidence: This is a fundamental assumption of the model for non-adopted individuals.

claim: More than 7000 individuals in the UK Biobank study report being adopted.
source: This is potentially important given that >7000 individuals in the UK Biobank study (Sudlow et al., 2015) report being adopted, and hence this publicly available dataset may represent a powerful resource for identifying prenatal maternal effects and partitioning maternal genetic effects into prenatal and postnatal sources of variation.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the UK Biobank dataset, supported by a citation.

claim: The covariance between an adopted individual's genotype and phenotype is a function of prenatal (but not postnatal) maternal genetic effects.
source: The intuition behind this surprising fact is that the covariance between an adopted individual's genotype and phenotype is a function of prenatal (but not postnatal) maternal genetic effects (Figure 1, G5 to G7).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the model structure, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The covariance between a non-adopted individual and their own phenotype includes contributions from prenatal and postnatal genetic effects.
source: In contrast, the covariance between a non-adopted individual and their own phenotype includes contributions from prenatal and postnatal genetic effects (Figure 1, G1 to G4).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the model structure for non-adopted individuals, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: The difference between the genotype-phenotype covariance in adopted and non-adopted singleton individuals provides important information on the likely size of postnatal genetic effects.
source: Thus, the difference between the genotype-phenotype covariance in adopted and non-adopted singleton individuals provides important information on the likely size of postnatal genetic effects.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the model structure.

claim: The power to detect prenatal maternal genetic effects increased with increasing size of postnatal maternal genetic effects, paternal genetic effects, and offspring genetic effects.
source: The power to detect prenatal maternal genetic effects increased with increasing size of postnatal maternal genetic effects, paternal genetic effects, and offspring genetic effects (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from power calculations, illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: The power to detect prenatal and postnatal maternal genetic effects increased with the number of adopted singleton individuals.
source: The power to detect prenatal and postnatal maternal genetic effects increased with the number of adopted singleton individuals, and more dramatically when the number of adoptive mother-adopted offspring pairs and/or biological mother-adopted offspring pairs increased (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from power calculations, illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: Power to detect prenatal maternal genetic effects increased most rapidly with increasing numbers of biological-mother adopted child pairs.
source: Power to detect prenatal maternal genetic effects increased most rapidly with increasing numbers of biological-mother adopted child pairs (G7), whereas the power to detect postnatal maternal genetic effects increased most strongly with increasing numbers of was provided by adoptive mother-adopted child pairs (G6).
evidence: This is a finding from power calculations.

claim: The power to detect postnatal maternal genetic effects increased most strongly with increasing numbers of adoptive mother-adopted child pairs.
source: Power to detect prenatal maternal genetic effects increased most rapidly with increasing numbers of biological-mother adopted child pairs (G7), whereas the power to detect postnatal maternal genetic effects increased most strongly with increasing numbers of was provided by adoptive mother-adopted child pairs (G6).
evidence: This is a finding from power calculations.

claim: The power to detect prenatal and postnatal maternal genetic effects also increased with the number of biological families in the analysis.
source: Interestingly, the power to detect prenatal and postnatal maternal genetic effects also increased with the number of biological families in the analysis (G1 to G4) (Figure 3); however, this increase asymptoted with maximal possible power depending primarily on the number of adopted individuals in the analysis.
evidence: This is a finding from power calculations, illustrated in Figure 3.

claim: Results from simulations showed good concordance with asymptotic power calculations and appropriate type I error rates.
source: Results from simulations showed good concordance with asymptotic power calculations and appropriate type I error rates (Supplementary file 3, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a validation finding from simulation studies.

claim: PRS for birth weight exhibited significant evidence of prenatal maternal genetic effects.
source: PRS for birth weight exhibited significant evidence of prenatal maternal genetic effects, offspring genetic effects (in the opposite direction), and no significant evidence for postnatal maternal or paternal genetic effects (Table 1).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from UK Biobank analysis, shown in Table 1.

claim: PRS for birth weight exhibited significant evidence of offspring genetic effects in the opposite direction to maternal effects.
source: PRS for birth weight exhibited significant evidence of prenatal maternal genetic effects, offspring genetic effects (in the opposite direction), and no significant evidence for postnatal maternal or paternal genetic effects (Table 1).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from UK Biobank analysis, shown in Table 1.

claim: PRS for birth weight showed no significant evidence for postnatal maternal or paternal genetic effects.
source: PRS for birth weight exhibited significant evidence of prenatal maternal genetic effects, offspring genetic effects (in the opposite direction), and no significant evidence for postnatal maternal or paternal genetic effects (Table 1).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from UK Biobank analysis, shown in Table 1.

claim: Birth weight is known to be affected by both maternal and fetal genetic effects.
source: This pattern of results is expected since (a) birth weight is known to be affected by both maternal and fetal genetic effects, (b) maternal and offspring genetic effects on birth weight for many of the SNPs were in opposite directions, (c) conditional estimates of maternal and offspring genetic effects are negatively correlated, (d) in the present study SNPs comprising the PRS were selected for their strong maternal effects on offspring birth weight, and (e) birth weight is a perinatal phenotype and so by definition cannot be influenced by postnatal maternal (or paternal) genetic effects (Warrington et al., 2019; Beaumont et al., 2018; Warrington et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Birth weight is a perinatal phenotype and so by definition cannot be influenced by postnatal maternal or paternal genetic effects.
source: This pattern of results is expected since (a) birth weight is known to be affected by both maternal and fetal genetic effects, (b) maternal and offspring genetic effects on birth weight for many of the SNPs were in opposite directions, (c) conditional estimates of maternal and offspring genetic effects are negatively correlated, (d) in the present study SNPs comprising the PRS were selected for their strong maternal effects on offspring birth weight, and (e) birth weight is a perinatal phenotype and so by definition cannot be influenced by postnatal maternal (or paternal) genetic effects (Warrington et al., 2019; Beaumont et al., 2018; Warrington et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a logical statement about the nature of birth weight as a phenotype, supported by citations.

claim: Analyses of offspring educational attainment showed evidence for a prenatal maternal genetic effect, a paternal genetic effect, and an offspring genetic effect.
source: In the case of offspring educational attainment, our analyses showed evidence for a prenatal maternal genetic effect, a paternal genetic effect, and an offspring genetic effect (Table 2, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from UK Biobank analysis, shown in Table 2.

claim: The absence of a significant positive postnatal maternal genetic effect on offspring educational attainment was surprising.
source: The absence of a significant positive postnatal maternal genetic effect on offspring educational attainment was surprising given that maternal genetic effects should be mediated through maternal educational attainment, and therefore should mostly involve postnatal pathways (although it is possible that some of the relationship between maternal genotype and offspring educational attainment could be mediated through prenatal effects- e.g. less educated mothers consuming more alcohol during pregnancy which then has adverse effects on offspring cognitive development and educational attainment etc), and previous studies have shown that the effect of paternal and maternal PRS on educational attainment are roughly similar (Wang et al., 2021) that is suggesting the absence of prenatal maternal genetic effects.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the empirical findings in the context of prior expectations.

claim: Previous studies have shown that the effect of paternal and maternal PRS on educational attainment are roughly similar.
source: The absence of a significant positive postnatal maternal genetic effect on offspring educational attainment was surprising given that maternal genetic effects should be mediated through maternal educational attainment, and therefore should mostly involve postnatal pathways (although it is possible that some of the relationship between maternal genotype and offspring educational attainment could be mediated through prenatal effects- e.g. less educated mothers consuming more alcohol during pregnancy which then has adverse effects on offspring cognitive development and educational attainment etc), and previous studies have shown that the effect of paternal and maternal PRS on educational attainment are roughly similar (Wang et al., 2021) that is suggesting the absence of prenatal maternal genetic effects.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2021.

claim: When adopted individuals with breastfeeding information were excluded, estimates of the prenatal maternal genetic effect on educational attainment reduced in size and became non-significant.
source: The results of these analyses showed that estimates of the prenatal maternal genetic effect reduced in size and became non-significant.
evidence: This is a finding from sensitivity analyses.

claim: The presence of adoptive parents who were genetically related to their adopted offspring could increase the type 1 error rate to detect prenatal maternal genetic effects and bias estimates when these relationships were not accurately modelled in the SEM.
source: Our simulations showed that the presence of adoptive parents who were genetically related to their adopted offspring could in some cases increase the type 1 error rate to detect prenatal maternal genetic effects and bias estimates of prenatal and postnatal maternal genetic effects when these relationships were not accurately modelled in the SEM (Appendix 1—figure 3, Appendix 1—figure 4, Appendix 1—figure 5, Appendix 1—figure 6).
evidence: This is a finding from simulation studies.

claim: When the relationship between biological and adoptive parents' genotypes was correctly modelled, there was no inflation in type 1 error rates and effect estimates were unbiased.
source: When we correctly modelled the relationship between biological and adoptive parents' genotypes, there was no inflation in type 1 error rates and effect estimates were unbiased (Appendix 1—figure 7, Appendix 1—figure 8, Appendix 1—figure 9, Appendix 1—figure 10).
evidence: This is a finding from simulation studies.

claim: Genetic studies of adopted individuals have a venerable history in the field of behavior genetics.
source: Genetic studies of adopted individuals have a venerable history in the field of behavior genetics (Leahy, 1935; Richardson, 1913).
evidence: This statement is supported by historical citations.

claim: Large studies of adopted individuals played a valuable role in resolving the 'Nature vs Nurture' debate of last century.
source: Indeed, large studies of adopted individuals played a valuable role in resolving the 'Nature vs Nurture' debate of last century, complementing similar findings from twin studies and other pedigree-based designs (Horn, 1983; Rhea et al., 2013; Scarr and Weinberg, 1983).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to adoption studies.

claim: The method provides point estimates and tests of the significance of prenatal and postnatal maternal genetic effects.
source: Second, our method provides point estimates and tests of the significance of prenatal and postnatal maternal genetic effects.
evidence: This is a description of the methodological capabilities of the approach.

claim: Cheesman et al., 2020 found that a genome-wide PRS for educational attainment was more strongly associated with educational attainment in non-adopted compared to adopted individuals.
source: The authors found that a genome-wide PRS for educational attainment was more strongly associated with educational attainment in non-adopted compared to adopted individuals consistent with the existence of indirect genetic effects on educational attainment.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited study.

claim: G-REML estimates of SNP heritability were lower in adopted individuals compared to non-adopted individuals.
source: Likewise, G-REML estimates of SNP heritability were also lower in adopted individuals compared to non-adopted individuals (potentially due to the absence/lower amount of passive gene-environment correlation in adopted individuals).
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Cheesman et al., 2020.

claim: Demange et al., 2020 found that estimates of indirect effects using the adoption study design were lower than those produced by sibling-based and trio-based models.
source: In general, the authors found that estimates of indirect effects using the adoption study design were lower than those produced by the other two models.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from a cited study.

claim: The number of adopted individuals in the UK Biobank is unlikely to be sufficient to resolve effects at individual genetic loci.
source: Our power calculations show that in principle the number of adopted individuals in the UK Biobank is unlikely to be sufficient to resolve effects at individual genetic loci but may be large enough to detect evidence for prenatal/postnatal maternal genetic effects in the case of PRS.
evidence: This is a conclusion from power calculations.

claim: The number of adopted individuals in the UK Biobank may be large enough to detect evidence for prenatal/postnatal maternal genetic effects in the case of PRS.
source: Our power calculations show that in principle the number of adopted individuals in the UK Biobank is unlikely to be sufficient to resolve effects at individual genetic loci but may be large enough to detect evidence for prenatal/postnatal maternal genetic effects in the case of PRS.
evidence: This is a conclusion from power calculations.

claim: The most efficient way to increase the power to detect prenatal and/or postnatal maternal genetic effects is to genotype adoptive mother-adopted child pairs and/or biological mother-adopted child pairs.
source: Regardless, the most efficient way to increase the power to detect prenatal and/or postnatal maternal genetic effects is to genotype adoptive mother-adopted child pairs and/or biological mother-adopted child pairs.
evidence: This is a conclusion from power calculations.

claim: Parental educational attainment is known to causally affect offspring educational attainment.
source: Parental educational attainment is known to causally affect offspring educational attainment (Bates et al., 2018; Kong et al., 2018; Hwang et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: It is not credible that prenatal mechanisms would lead to larger effect sizes than postnatal pathways for educational attainment.
source: Whilst it is possible, even probable, that some loci may affect offspring educational attainment through prenatal maternal pathways, it is not credible that such mechanisms would lead to larger effect sizes than those from postnatal pathways, or that fathers would exhibit strong evidence of postnatal effects but not mothers.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the nature of educational attainment.

claim: Substantial numbers of adopted individuals in the UK Biobank may have been raised by their biological relatives.
source: Rather we hypothesize it is possible that our model could have been misspecified in that substantial numbers of adopted individuals in the UK Biobank may have in fact been raised by their biological relatives.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain unexpected findings.

claim: Sensitivity analyses that excluded adopted individuals with known breastfeeding information suggested that including adopted individuals who were raised by genetically related adoptive mothers may lead to inflated prenatal maternal genetic effect estimates.
source: Sensitivity analyses that excluded adopted individuals with known breastfeeding information suggested that including adopted individuals who were raised by genetically related adoptive mothers may lead to inflated prenatal maternal genetic effect estimates.
evidence: This is a conclusion from sensitivity analyses.

claim: Some studies have reported that adoptive families are better educated and have higher socio-economic status than the population average.
source: For example, some studies have reported that adoptive families are better educated and have higher socio-economic status than the population average (Kendler et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: There is limited evidence for large genotype by environment interactions at individual genetic loci.
source: In contrast, in our design it is more important that genetic effect sizes are homogenous across adopted and non-adopted individuals (i.e. no genotype by environment interaction), and at least currently, there is limited evidence for large genotype by environment interactions at individual genetic loci.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of evidence in the field.

claim: Accurately modelling cryptic relationships does not require that actual genotypes for adoptive and/or biological parents be obtained.
source: We emphasize that accurately modelling these relationships does not require that actual genotypes for adoptive and/or biological parents be obtained (although this would be advantageous in terms of statistical power) as our SEM allows us to model these relationships in terms of latent variables.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of the SEM approach.

claim: Spousal correlations for educational attainment phenotype in complete parent-offspring trios in the UK Biobank is r=0.285.
source: Spousal correlations for phenotypes (educational attainment: r=0.285; birth weight: r=0.076) and PRS (educational attainment: r=0.117; birth weight: r=0.068) in complete parent-offspring trios in the UK Biobank suggest that assortative mating is likely present for educational attainment, and potentially to a lesser degree for (phenotypes correlated with) birth weight.
evidence: This is an empirical observation from UK Biobank data.

claim: Spousal correlations for birth weight phenotype in complete parent-offspring trios in the UK Biobank is r=0.076.
source: Spousal correlations for phenotypes (educational attainment: r=0.285; birth weight: r=0.076) and PRS (educational attainment: r=0.117; birth weight: r=0.068) in complete parent-offspring trios in the UK Biobank suggest that assortative mating is likely present for educational attainment, and potentially to a lesser degree for (phenotypes correlated with) birth weight.
evidence: This is an empirical observation from UK Biobank data.

claim: Spousal correlations for educational attainment PRS in complete parent-offspring trios in the UK Biobank is r=0.117.
source: Spousal correlations for phenotypes (educational attainment: r=0.285; birth weight: r=0.076) and PRS (educational attainment: r=0.117; birth weight: r=0.068) in complete parent-offspring trios in the UK Biobank suggest that assortative mating is likely present for educational attainment, and potentially to a lesser degree for (phenotypes correlated with) birth weight.
evidence: This is an empirical observation from UK Biobank data.

claim: Spousal correlations for birth weight PRS in complete parent-offspring trios in the UK Biobank is r=0.068.
source: Spousal correlations for phenotypes (educational attainment: r=0.285; birth weight: r=0.076) and PRS (educational attainment: r=0.117; birth weight: r=0.068) in complete parent-offspring trios in the UK Biobank suggest that assortative mating is likely present for educational attainment, and potentially to a lesser degree for (phenotypes correlated with) birth weight.
evidence: This is an empirical observation from UK Biobank data.

claim: Assortative mating is likely present for educational attainment in the UK Biobank.
source: Spousal correlations for phenotypes (educational attainment: r=0.285; birth weight: r=0.076) and PRS (educational attainment: r=0.117; birth weight: r=0.068) in complete parent-offspring trios in the UK Biobank suggest that assortative mating is likely present for educational attainment, and potentially to a lesser degree for (phenotypes correlated with) birth weight.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed spousal correlations.

claim: The presence of latent horizontal pleiotropy is one of the major threats to the validity of causal inference from MR studies.
source: The presence of latent horizontal pleiotropy is one of the major threats to the validity of causal inference from MR studies (Hemani et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: The covariance between adoptive mother's genotype and offspring phenotype should provide an estimate of genetic effects due to postnatal horizontal genetic pleiotropy.
source: Consequently, if the focus of an MR study is on estimating the causal effect of a prenatal maternal exposure on an offspring outcome, the covariance between adoptive mother's genotype and offspring (outcome) phenotype should provide an estimate of genetic effects due to postnatal horizontal genetic pleiotropy.
evidence: This is a logical inference about how the model could be applied to MR studies.

claim: The approach will not correct for the effect of prenatal/early life horizontal pleiotropy in MR studies.
source: It is important to realize, however, that this procedure will not correct for the effect of prenatal/early life horizontal pleiotropy as these paths will be present in both biological and adopted individuals and so this approach is not a panacea for dealing with latent pleiotropy in MR studies.
evidence: This is a limitation of the proposed approach for MR studies.

claim: There would be considerable value in following up adopted individuals in the UK Biobank to determine whether they were raised by biological relatives.
source: We conclude that there would be considerable value in following up adopted individuals in the UK Biobank to determine whether they were raised by biological relatives, and if so, to precisely ascertain the nature of the relationship.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study.

claim: The UK Biobank study was approved by the UK National Health Service National Research Ethics Service.
source: The UK Biobank study was approved by the UK National Health Service National Research Ethics Service.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: This study was approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee at the University of Queensland (approval number: 2019002705).
source: This study was approved by the Human Research Ethics Committee at the University of Queensland (approval number: 2019002705).
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Only individuals of European ancestry were included in the UK Biobank analyses.
source: We only included individuals of European ancestry, determined by: (i) projecting their genetic principal components onto the 1,000 Genome sample and then K-means clustering or (ii) those who self-reported ethnic background of either 'British', 'Irish', 'Irish', 'White', or 'Any other white background'.
evidence: This is a description of the sample selection criteria.

claim: Family relationships in the UK Biobank were determined using the software KING.
source: Family relationships were determined by the pairwise kinship estimated across the whole UK Biobank sample using the software KING (Manichaikul et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a description of the methodology used, supported by a citation.

claim: The birth weight analysis included 731 biological trios, 2014 biological mother-offspring pairs, 485 biological father-offspring pairs, 168,522 singletons raised by their biological parents, 1084 singleton individuals who reported being adopted, and 16 biological mother-adopted offspring pairs.
source: These included 731 biological trios, 2014 biological mother-offspring pairs, 485 biological father-offspring pairs, 168,522 singletons raised by their biological parents, 1084 singleton individuals who reported being adopted, and 16 biological mother-adopted offspring pairs.
evidence: This is a description of the sample composition for the birth weight analysis.

claim: 20 SNPs known to influence birth weight via maternal pathways with p<5 x 10–8 were used to construct PRS for birth weight.
source: We calculated each individual's weighted PRS (i.e. sums of the birth weight-increasing allele weighted by the effect size) and unweighted PRS (i.e. counts of the birth weight increasing allele) for birth weight using 20 SNPs known to influence birth weight via maternal pathways with p<5 x 10–8 from a recent GWAS of birth weight (Warrington et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a description of the PRS construction methodology, supported by a citation.

claim: The educational attainment analysis included 943 biological parent-offspring trios, 2687 biological mother-offspring pairs, 712 biological father-offspring pairs, 347,980 singletons from biological families, 5178 adopted singletons and 39 biological mother-adopted offspring pairs.
source: The final dataset included 943 biological parent-offspring trios, 2687 biological mother-offspring pairs, 712 biological father-offspring pairs, 347,980 singletons from biological families, 5178 adopted singletons and 39 biological mother-adopted offspring pairs.
evidence: This is a description of the sample composition for the educational attainment analysis.

claim: 1267 SNPs from the current largest GWAS of educational attainment were used to construct PRS for educational attainment.
source: We calculated weighted PRS (i.e. sums of the educational attainment increasing allele and weighted by the effect size) and unweighted PRS (i.e. counts of the educational attainment increasing allele) using 1267 SNPs from the current largest GWAS of educational attainment (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a description of the PRS construction methodology, supported by a citation.

claim: Only genome-wide significant SNPs were included in the construction of educational attainment PRS because the most recent GWAS meta-analysis included UK Biobank individuals.
source: We included only genome-wide significant SNPs in the construction of these scores because the most recent GWAS meta-analysis of educational attainment by Lee et al., 2018 included UK Biobank individuals (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an explanation of the methodological choice to avoid sample overlap bias.

claim: A sensitivity analysis was performed using a second set of PRS of educational attainment using 72 SNPs from a GWAS of non-UK Biobank individuals.
source: For this reason, we also performed a sensitivity analysis using a second set of PRS of educational attainment using 72 SNPs from a GWAS of non-UK Biobank individuals (Okbay et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a description of a sensitivity analysis performed, supported by a citation.

claim: Excluding adopted individuals with known breastfeeding information reduced the number of adopted 'singleton' individuals in the educational attainment analysis to 2,867.
source: This reduced the number of adopted 'singleton' individuals in the analysis to 2,867.
evidence: This is a description of the effect of the sensitivity analysis on sample size.

claim: The model assumes that the effect of the prenatal maternal genetic effect and postnatal maternal genetic effect on the offspring phenotype is additive.
source: We are specifically interested in partitioning maternal genetic effects into prenatal (γm) and postnatal genetic effects (ϐm) and we assume that the effect of the prenatal maternal genetic effect and postnatal maternal genetic effect on the offspring phenotype is additive (i.e. γm + ϐm).
evidence: This is a fundamental assumption of the model.

claim: The model assumes that biological fathers exert only postnatal genetic effects on their offspring.
source: We assume that biological fathers exert only postnatal genetic effects on their offspring (biological families only), and adoptive fathers exert only postnatal genetic effects on their adopted offspring.
evidence: This is a fundamental assumption of the model.

claim: The model assumes that adoptive fathers exert only postnatal genetic effects on their adopted offspring.
source: We assume that biological fathers exert only postnatal genetic effects on their offspring (biological families only), and adoptive fathers exert only postnatal genetic effects on their adopted offspring.
evidence: This is a fundamental assumption of the model.

claim: The model permits the variance of residual sources of variation to differ across adopted and biological family structures.
source: Finally, to accommodate the possibility that adopted individuals may have different phenotypic variances to individuals raised by their biological relatives, we permit the variance of residual sources of variation to differ across adopted and biological family structures (Cheesman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a feature of the model design, supported by a citation.

claim: For all the parameters in the model to be identified, different constellations of relatives must be sampled from G1-G7.
source: We caution that for all the parameters in the model to be identified, different constellations of relatives must be sampled from G1-G7.
evidence: This is a statement about the requirements for model identifiability.

claim: To partition maternal genetic effects into prenatal and postnatal components, information from adopted individuals must be available.
source: For example, to partition maternal genetic effects into prenatal and postnatal components, information from adopted individuals must be available.
evidence: This is a statement about the requirements for partitioning maternal genetic effects.

claim: The inclusion of adopted singleton individuals in the model is sufficient for identification as long as there are at least some biological parent-offspring trios or both biological mother-child and biological father-child pairs available.
source: Indeed, the inclusion of adopted singleton individuals in our model is sufficient for identification as long as there are at least some (biological) parent-offspring trios (or alternatively both biological mother-child and biological father-child pairs) available.
evidence: This is a statement about the minimum requirements for model identification.

claim: The presence of adopted individuals' parents (biological or adoptive) is not a necessary condition for partitioning maternal effects into prenatal and postnatal components.
source: Whilst the presence of adopted individuals' parents (biological or adoptive) is not a necessary condition for partitioning maternal effects into prenatal and postnatal components, the inclusion of such pairs is advantageous in terms of statistical power as we show below.
evidence: This is a statement about model requirements and power.

claim: The inclusion of adopted individuals' parents is advantageous in terms of statistical power.
source: Whilst the presence of adopted individuals' parents (biological or adoptive) is not a necessary condition for partitioning maternal effects into prenatal and postnatal components, the inclusion of such pairs is advantageous in terms of statistical power as we show below.
evidence: This is a statement about statistical power, supported by results shown later.

claim: OpenMx was used to calculate the asymptotic power to partition maternal genetic effects into prenatal and postnatal maternal genetic effects.
source: We used OpenMx (Boker et al., 2011; Neale et al., 2016) to calculate the asymptotic power to partition maternal genetic effects into prenatal and postnatal maternal genetic effects.
evidence: This is a description of the software used for power calculations, supported by citations.

claim: A freely available online power calculator was developed that allows investigators to explore the power to detect prenatal and postnatal maternal genetic effects using the SEM.
source: We developed a freely available, online power calculator that allows investigators to explore the power to detect prenatal and postnatal maternal genetic effects using our SEM in their own studies (https://evansgroup.di.uq.edu.au/ADOPTED).

claim: The power calculator is built using the R shiny app running the R studio software and the OpenMx package.
source: Our power calculator is built using the R shiny app (https://shiny.rstudio.com/) running the R studio software (RStudioTeam, 2015) and the OpenMx package (Boker et al., 2011; Neale et al., 2016) in the background.
evidence: This is a description of the technical implementation of the power calculator.

claim: Adopted singleton individuals provide important information on partitioning maternal genetic effects regardless of whether information on their parents has been gathered.
source: It is important to realize, however, that adopted 'singletons' (i.e. adopted individuals whose adoptive and biological parents have not been included in the study) provide important information on partitioning maternal genetic effects into prenatal and postnatal contributions regardless of whether information on their parents has been gathered.
evidence: This is a key insight about the value of adopted singleton data.

claim: The effect of inadvertently including adopted singleton individuals whose adoptive parents are genetically related to them was investigated.
source: We investigate the effect of inadvertently including adopted singleton individuals whose adoptive parents are genetically related to them in our model, adjust our model to correct for this misspecification and quantify the effect of this adjustment on type 1 error rates and power.
evidence: This is a description of analyses performed in the study.
